title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: Beanie Babies: Reigning Toy Craze Champion
summary: A holiday-season playlist episode of Stuff You Should Know on Beanie Babies, the 1990s plush toy craze created by Ty Warner. The hosts cover Warner's background and firing from his sales job, the 1993 launch of Beanie Babies at five dollars with birth dates and poems on heart-shaped tags, the limited-distribution marketing scheme, the 1995 Beanie Babies website and early e-commerce, retirement-driven scarcity, the 1998 McDonald's Teenie Beanies promotion, the speculative secondary market and price guides, crime and divorce stories tied to the craze, the 1999 retirement announcement and later revival, the bubble's collapse, Warner's tax evasion case and Swiss account, and the 2023-era movie The Beanie Bubble. Listener mail is skipped; the hosts close with tour dates and warnings about scalper sites and gift-card scams.
topics: Beanie Baby divorce case Las Vegas

segments.title: Cold open teaser
segments.summary: Josh previews the episode on Beanie Babies, a playlist pick placed before the Christmas episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Beanie Baby bubble
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the classic toy episode tradition and call the Beanie Baby craze of the mid-to-late 1990s possibly the greatest market bubble, with adults rather than kids driving demand.

segments.title: Ty Warner's early life and sales career
segments.summary: Ty Warner, born in the mid-1940s in LaGrange, Illinois, had a difficult childhood, attended Kalamazoo College, and became a flamboyant salesman for his father's toy company starting in 1962.

segments.title: Warner's firing
segments.summary: Warner was fired in 1980 by CEO Harold Nazamian, who accused him of using company sales lists and time to sell his own products.

segments.title: Plush cats and the move to toys
segments.summary: After living in Rome for a few years, Warner created a line of named, fully stuffed plush cats such as Smoky and Peaches, priced at about twenty dollars.

segments.title: Beanie Baby design, bean stuffing and pricing
segments.summary: Beanie Babies were stuffed with beads rather than foam pellets so they could be posed, were made with South Korean manufacturers under Warner's close design involvement, and sold for about five dollars aimed at kids' allowances.

segments.title: 1993 launch and tag marketing
segments.summary: Beanie Babies launched in 1993 with Brownie the bear and Pinchers the lobster; each came with a birth date and a poem on a heart-shaped tag, a marketing touch similar to Cabbage Patch Kids adoption papers.

segments.title: Limited retail distribution
segments.summary: Beanie Babies were sold only through licensed retailers such as Hallmark stores, gift shops and hospital shops, not big box stores, creating status and exclusivity.

segments.title: Scarcity through limited allocations
segments.summary: Warner limited how many Beanie Babies each store could buy and assigned different models to different stores, pushing kids to hunt for complete collections.

segments.title: Retirements and the early website
segments.summary: Warner deliberately retired models, sometimes abruptly, creating real scarcity; the company's coder Lena Trevetti pushed for a Beanie Babies website, which began online sales in 1995, the same year as eBay and Amazon.

segments.title: The Beanie Bubble movie and credit for women
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 2023 film The Beanie Bubble, its fictionalized characters based on Zac Bissonnette's book, and the unacknowledged contributions of women at the company.

segments.title: Secrecy and manufactured scarcity
segments.summary: Warner kept production numbers secret and announced retirements on the website, prompting collectors to rush to stores; retailers stockpiled retired models such as the orange Pinchers.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before the McDonald's segment.

segments.title: McDonald's Teenie Beanies promotion
segments.summary: McDonald's 1997 and 1998 Happy Meal promotions with Teenie Beanies drove record sales; customers ordered many meals and franchises set purchase limits.

segments.title: Cultural and comparisons to McRib
segments.summary: The hosts compare the Teenie Beanies sales record to the McRib and riff on false scarcity.

segments.title: Beanie Babies as investment and eBay boom
segments.summary: Many adults treated Beanie Babies as an investment; by 1997 about six percent of eBay sales were Beanie Babies and retired pieces sold for hundreds of dollars.

segments.title: Price guides and collector authorities
segments.summary: Peggy Gallagher self-published a book, and Mary Beth Sobaluski produced the price guide and Mary Beth Bean Bag World magazine, with suburban Chicago soccer moms helping start the trading trend; HBO documentary Beanie Bubble Mania is mentioned.

segments.title: 1999 Las Vegas divorce beanie split
segments.summary: A 1999 Las Vegas divorce case required the couple to divide their Beanie Babies on the courtroom floor one at a time, a process the wife described as demoralizing.
topics: Beanie Baby divorce case Las Vegas

segments.title: Chris Robinson Senior and Bankrupted by Beanies
segments.summary: Chris Robinson Senior bought about 20,000 Beanie Babies for roughly 100,000 dollars; his son made the short documentary Bankrupted by Beanies.

segments.title: Beanie Baby crime and murder
segments.summary: Counterfeiting and non-delivery fraud occurred; Ben Perry was charged with stealing about 1,300 Beanie Babies and became the Beanie Baby Bandit; Jeffrey White killed Harry Simmons in West Virginia in a dispute tied to borrowed Beanie Babies.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before wrapping up the story.

segments.title: Retirement of 1999 and the 2000 revote
segments.summary: The website announced in August 1999 that production would stop; Warner later reversed course on Christmas Eve, letting fans vote for fifty cents each with proceeds to a pediatric AIDS foundation, and 91 percent voted to continue.

segments.title: Collapse of the bubble and Princess Diana Beanie
segments.summary: The line continued until about 2002 but collapsed as people realized common Beanies, including the Princess Diana bear, were not scarce; the hosts compare the bubble to Bitcoin.

segments.title: Ty Warner's wealth, flex ad and tax case
segments.summary: Warner took out a Wall Street Journal ad claiming 700 million dollars in 1997 profits; he later pleaded to tax evasion over a Swiss bank account, receiving probation, community service, a fine, and civil penalties.

segments.title: Later business and hotel
segments.summary: Ty Inc. expanded into licensing with Garfield and Disney, and Warner owns the New York Four Seasons, which is closed amid a dispute with the brand; he also donated during COVID for first responders.

segments.title: Secondary market scams and gift-card warnings
segments.summary: Hosts warn about inflated eBay listings and scammers who demand gift-card payment, and banter about the film casting.

segments.title: Listener mail skipped and tour announcement
segments.summary: Listener mail is skipped this week; the hosts promote live shows and tickets from legitimate sellers.
